paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A convergent boundary is a place where two or more of Earth's lithospheric plates collide. It is also called a destructive boundary. Eventually one plate slides beneath the other, a process called subduction. These collisions play out over millions to tens of millions of years. They can lead to volcanism, earthquakes, mountain building, destruction of lithosphere and deformation.

paragraphs.heading: Why one plate sinks
paragraphs.text: Convection in the mantle brings hot material up to the surface along spreading centers, where it makes new crust. Newer crust then forms and pushes this crust away from the spreading center, and as it goes it cools, thins and becomes denser. Subduction starts when that dense crust meets a crust that is less dense. The force of gravity helps to drive the subducting slab down into the mantle.

paragraphs.heading: Water, melting and volcanoes
paragraphs.text: The subducting slab is relatively cool, and it is heated as it sinks deeper into the mantle. The oceanic crust contains hydrous minerals, such as the amphibole and mica groups, and the heating breaks them down. That releases water into the hotter asthenosphere. The water lowers the melting temperature of rocks there and causes partial melting. Both the loss of water and the partial melting take place along the 1,000 °C isotherm, usually 65 to 130 km down. Where the resulting magmas reach the surface, they create volcanic arcs.

paragraphs.heading: Three kinds of collision
paragraphs.text: Convergent boundaries occur in three pairings: oceanic with oceanic lithosphere, oceanic with continental, and continental with continental. The geologic features vary with the types of crust involved. When two oceanic plates collide, the cooler, denser one sinks beneath the warmer, less dense one, and partial melt eventually reaches the surface and forms volcanic island arcs. When oceanic and continental lithosphere collide, the dense oceanic lithosphere goes under the less dense continental lithosphere. Deep-sea sediments and oceanic crust are scraped off the oceanic plate and form an accretionary wedge on the continental crust. Volcanic arcs form on the continental lithosphere.

paragraphs.heading: When a continent arrives
paragraphs.text: Some plates consist of both continental and oceanic crust. As the oceanic part subducts to greater depths, the continental crust attached to it is pulled closer to the subduction zone. Once continental lithosphere reaches the zone, the process changes, because continental lithosphere is more buoyant and resists going under other continental lithosphere. A little of the continental crust may be subducted before the slab breaks. The oceanic lithosphere can then keep subducting, hot asthenosphere rises to fill the void, and the continental lithosphere rebounds.

paragraphs.heading: The evidence underground
paragraphs.text: Subduction zones often have an abundance of earthquakes, and the plane where many of them occur is called the Wadati–Benioff zone. Earthquakes have been detected as deep as 670 km. Seismic records have been used to map torn slabs beneath the Caucasus, where two continents converge. Ultrahigh pressure metamorphic rocks, which form 90 to 125 km down, are exposed at the surface, and they are evidence of the continental rebound.
